briefings.title: AI as research analyst versus AI as participant
briefings.dek: Teams must decide whether to use AI to process what real participants say, to replace the participants, or neither.
briefings.scenario: A research team at a large retailer has a slow recruitment pipeline and a backlog of unread survey comments and interview notes. Leadership asks whether AI-generated users and automated synthesis can cut both the cost and the wait.

positions.label: Start with analysis work
positions.summary: One piece revisits an earlier bet that coding open-ended survey comments is a good job for AI, since those comments often get only a cursory look. Another describes rebuilding a product around interview synthesis, and says the hard part was the evaluation and repair machinery around the agents, not the agents themselves.

positions.label: Test synthetic participants first
positions.summary: This piece starts from the cost and delay of recruitment and the appeal of AI that mimics participants' attitudes. It checks that appeal against a concrete benchmark, SUS scores, rather than assuming the substitution works.

briefings.context: Recruitment is a major cost in research budgets, so the pull toward synthetic users is strong. Coding open-ended responses and synthesizing interviews are analysis steps that still start from real participant data. Replacing the participants removes that grounding, so it needs a different standard of proof.

steps.label: Baseline against humans
steps.text: Before trusting AI coding or synthesis, compare its output with a human-coded sample from the same data.

steps.label: Build evals early
steps.text: Budget time for evaluation and correction steps around any automated synthesis, since the surrounding checks may be the hard part.

steps.label: Validate synthetic users
steps.text: Run synthetic participants alongside a real study and compare their results to known outcomes before they inform any decision.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts are truncated and give no results, so they don't show how accurate AI coding, synthesis, or digital twins actually were.

briefings.title: Delegating design work to agents has a price
briefings.dek: Teams must decide which design tasks to give to AI agents, knowing that each handoff may weaken the system, the skills, or the judgment behind it.
briefings.scenario: A design systems team at a large retailer is offered an agent that can update component libraries, draft specs, and give first-pass critique. Leaders want the speed, but the team worries that no one will understand the system after a year of agent-built changes.

positions.label: Delegate the routine, keep the craft
positions.summary: Figma presents the agent as a way to take over library updates, critique feedback, and first-draft specs so designers can concentrate on the core problem. It treats deciding what to hand off as a learnable skill and points to teams that report fast, high-quality work.

positions.label: Delegation erodes understanding
positions.summary: These pieces argue that cheap agent output leads to fragile systems that their owners no longer grasp, and to weaker thinking and taste. One author describes running many agents at once and losing the ability to see work as a whole.

briefings.context: Figma's agent is now generally available, so the question has moved from experiment to everyday practice. The critical pieces describe a different pattern: when producing is nearly free, people produce more, understand less, and lean on safe defaults. Both sides agree that judgment about what to delegate matters, but they disagree about whether the tools help build it or wear it down.

steps.label: Map the handoffs
steps.text: List the tasks in your workflow and mark which ones an agent could take, separating mechanical upkeep from decisions that shape the product.

steps.label: Keep a human owner
steps.text: Give every agent-touched artifact, such as a library or spec, a named person who can explain how it works without asking the agent.

steps.label: Protect practice time
steps.text: Set aside work that designers do by hand, and review it for taste and critique skills, so judgment is exercised rather than assumed.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts are short and the Figma pieces are vendor-authored, so none of them offers measured evidence on how much delegation actually degrades systems or skills over time.
